name: Larva-24010
iocPatterns: Infection via compromised software distribution sites
Deployment of MeshAgent and NKNShell backdoors
Use of Netcat variants for shell access
Leveraging mshta.exe for malicious script execution
Hosting on infrastructure masquerading as trusted VPN services
recommendedActions: Implement strict controls over the use of third-party VPN services on corporate networks.
Block known indicators associated with MeshAgent, NKNShell, and QuasarRAT.
Deploy endpoint detection (EDR) to monitor for suspicious mshta.exe or powershell.exe child processes.
Monitor network traffic for non-standard ports or unusual behavior from netcat utilities.
Implement application whitelisting to prevent the execution of unauthorized binaries from downloaded installers.
Conduct deep packet inspection (DPI) on traffic heading toward known VPN providers that have been flagged as compromised.
Audit system service configurations, specifically checking for suspicious 'systemd' or hidden services.
Educate employees on the risks of using unofficial or third-party software distribution channels.
campaignsText: Larva-24010 has been active since at least 2023, specifically targeting the South Korean VPN market to gain access to a wide variety of systems geographically and sectorally. Their tactic involves high volumes of compromise via trusted software installers, indicating an opportunistic but highly organized campaign structure focused on data harvesting from users who believe they are securing their online presence.
description: Larva-24010 is a sophisticated threat actor that leverages supply chain compromises, specifically by infecting the official website of a South Korean VPN provider, to distribute multiple backdoors. Since at least 2023, they have used this vector to deliver tools like MeshAgent and NKNShell for information theft against users seeking secure internet access.
goals: The primary stated motivation for Larva-24010 is financial gain through information theft. By targeting the VPN market, they strategically position themselves to compromise diverse users ranging from individual consumers to corporate employees in high-importance sectors such as energy, finance, and government. Their target profile encompasses a wide array of industries (military, manufacturing, etc.) in countries like South Korea, Japan, and various Western nations, suggesting a strategy focused on broad information harvesting rather than specific political espionage.
